title_r: Study 1 (Direct Replication)
abstract_r:
**CREP Project: #20-43** 
 
**PROTOCOL TITLE:**   
Evaluation of Meat Consumption 
 
**PRINCIPAL INVESTIGATOR (PI):**   
*Name:* Heather Urry   
*Department:* Psychology 
 
**Purpose of the study:** 
 
This study is a direct replication of one experiment from research conducted by Sparkman and Walton (2017) that investigated dynamic and static norms in relation to meat consumption. Our study aims to determine whether dynamic norms lead to a greater desire to change one’s eating habits than static norms.  
 
**Background / Literature Review / Rationale for the study:** 
 
In the original study by Sparkman and Walton (2017), the researchers found that participants were more interested in reducing their meat consumption if they first learned that norms for reducing meat consumption have been increasing over the past 5 years. This was compared to a condition in which there was no implied change; the norm was presented as static.  
 
We are replicating this study because the topic is of general interest and importance. In addition, this study is among those available for undergraduate student groups to replicate with faculty mentorship as part of the Collaborative Replications and Education Project.  
 
**Participant Population:** 
 
We will study adult participants currently in the United States who are at least 18 years old, each of whom may participate in the study just once. (Vegan/vegetarian participants will be excluded from analyses but not from participating in the study.) 
 
**Research Locations and Sample Size:** 
 
*Research Locations* 
 
This research will be administered online via a Qualtrics survey. Participants will complete it in a location of their choosing that offers a computer with internet access. 
 
*Sample Size* 
 
We seek to recruit at least 122 participants, the same number of participants studied by the original authors. A sample of 122 participants – 61 in each of two norm conditions – will give us 80% power to detect medium standardized effects of Cohen’s *d* = 0.51 or larger for the difference in self-reported interest between the dynamic and static conditions.   
 
The original authors reported an effect size of Cohen’s *d* = 0.41. Ideally we’d have enough participants to detect an effect of that size with adequate power in this study. This would require 94 participants per group for a total of 188 participants.   
 
Even better, we should have enough participants to detect an effect that’s so small that the original authors would have been unlikely to detect it. To that end, Simonsohn (2015) suggests specifying in one’s power analysis an effect size the original authors could have detected with only 33% power.  In this case, with 118 participants included in the key analysis, the original authors had 33% power to detect an effect size of Cohen’s *d* = 0.28.  To have 80% power to detect an effect size of *d* = 0.28 or larger, we would need to collect data from 201 participants per group for a total of 402 participants.  
 
Our maximum N will be 3,000.  
 
**Procedures Involved:** 
 
We are conducting a between-subjects experiment in which we will manipulate type of norm (dynamic, static). Participants will complete this research online via a Qualtrics survey. We anticipate that each participant will take 5-10 minutes to complete the study. The study will unfold over the course of the Fall 2020 semester.  
 
The survey will start by assessing the GeoIP location of potential respondents. For people whose GeoIP location suggests they are not currently in the United States, the survey will explain our eligibility criteria and then take the respondent to a message noting their ineligibility. Otherwise, the survey will proceed to the informed consent form. 
 
After providing informed consent, participants will respond to a Captcha verification item to prevent bot responses to the online survey. They will also provide answers to three eligibility items (age at least 18 years, have not participated before, and currently in the United States) to prevent participation by people who are ineligible. Participants who are ineligible or decline to answer will then see a message explaining that they are ineligible.  
 
Participants who are eligible will then read instructions related to their randomly-assigned norm condition. In the static-norm condition, participants will read: 
 
    Recent research has shown that 30% of Americans make an effort to limit their meat consumption. That means that 3 in 10 people eat less meat than they otherwise would.  
 
In the dynamic-norm condition, participants will read: 
 
    Recent research has shown that, in the last 5 years, 30% of Americans have now started to make an effort to limit their meat consumption. That means that, in recent years, 3 in 10 people have changed their behavior and begun to eat less meat than they otherwise would. 
 
After reading the statement, each participant will respond to the following items: 
 
1.	How interested are you in eating less meat? (1 = not at all, 4 = somewhat, 7 = extremely). 
2.	Most people eat breakfast, lunch and dinner everyday. That means they eat 21 meals in a typical week. For those that make an effort to eat less meat, how many times do you think they eat a meal without meat in a week? 
3.	What percentage of people do you think make an effort to limit their meat consumption? 
4.	Which best describes your political ideology? (1 = very liberal, 7 = very conservative) 
5.	What word or phrase best describes your gender?  
6.	Are you vegetarian or vegan? 
7.	What is your current age in years? 
8.	What word or phrase best describes your race and/or ethnicity? 
9.	Did you participate to earn SONA credit or for a chance to enter a drawing? (SONA credit, Drawing, Neither; I'm volunteering) 
 
Finally, participants will see the debriefing form and an item in which they will have the option to exclude their data from the final data set, if they wish.  
 
Some items will require a response from participants; they will always have a “decline to answer” option so they are not compelled to provide information they do not wish to share. 
 
Participants who say they took part for compensation in the form of entering a drawing will, upon clicking the survey submission button, be redirected to a new contact information survey in which they can provide their name and email address if they wish to be entered into a drawing to receive $50 as compensation. Participants who say they took part for compensation in the form of SONA credit will receive 0.5 credits in the SONA credit system. 
 
Some pages in the survey will be set to measure the time participants spend on them for exploratory analyses.   
 
**Confirmatory Analyses:** 
 
We will exclude from analyses participants who identify as vegetarian/vegan, participants who decline to include their responses in the final data set after debriefing, participants who select the "decline to answer" option for key variables in each analysis, and participants who do not complete the survey through to the debriefing form and thus do not have the opportunity to withdraw their data. 
 
After applying these exclusions, we will repeat the same analyses reported by Sparkman and Walton (2017) as follows:  
 
1.	A t-test to see if type of norm (dynamic, static) affects self-reported interest in reducing meat consumption.  
2.	A multiple regression to see if type of norm affects self-reported interest in reducing meat consumption when accounting for variation explained by gender and political orientation.  
3.	Two additional t-tests to see if type of norm (dynamic, static) affects estimates of the percentage of people who limit their meat consumption and the number of meatless meals per week eaten by people who say they limited their meat consumption. 
 
We will also report descriptive statistics and standardized effect sizes as reported by the original authors. 
 
In addition, we anticipate that there may be outlying observations or responses suggesting a lack of good-faith participation (e.g., based on open-ended information or extremely fast completion times). We may repeat our confirmatory analyses without these observations to see if conclusions change. 
 
**Known Deviations** 
 
1. We are recruiting participants in the United States, probably most of whom will be students at Tufts and/or people in the Boston area of Massachusetts. The original researchers recruited participants using Amazon's Mechanical Turk. 
2. We will offer participants the opportunity to enter a drawing for USD 50 dollars or to earn credit in partial fulfillment of course requirements as incentives to participate. In the original study, participants on Mechanical Turk received USD 25 cents. 
3. For our replication, the survey will include eligibility items (Captcha verification, age at least 18 years, have not participated before, and currently in the United States) before participants complete the survey items that address confirmatory hypotheses. 
 
**Incomplete Disclosure or Deception:** 
 
In the consent form, we tell participants that we are not disclosing all information about the nature and purpose of the study and that, at the end of the study, they’ll receive a full explanation. Specifically, we do not disclose our specific focus on whether dynamic versus static norms influence interest in reducing meat consumption, or that we’re measuring how much time they spend on various pages of the survey and other variables of interest, as described above. This incomplete disclosure is necessary because full participant knowledge could impact their responses and compromise our results. We do not believe this incomplete disclosure violates the rights or welfare of participants because a) we correctly inform potential participants in the consent form that we’re conducting a study to evaluate meat consumption, b) we correctly inform participants about the general procedures of the study, namely that they’ll be completing a survey and demographic items, and c) we will fully debrief participants afterwards, including providing them the opportunity to decline to include their responses in the final data set.  
 
**Recruitment Methods:** 
 
We will recruit a convenience sample of participants. Study personnel will recruit people they know by word of mouth in person or via email, or by posting an invitation to participate on social media such as Facebook, Twitter, or other websites, including the Psychology Department’s SONA paid system website. The materials note that we’re recruiting adults ages 18 years and up who are currently in the United States and have not participated in this research previously. We will also recruit participants via the Psychology Department’s SONA credit participant pool. Participants will earn 0.5 credits in partial fulfillment of departmental course requirements. 
 
**Consent Process:**  
 
Participants will provide informed consent by reading the consent form online and then clicking a button in the Qualtrics survey.  
 
To ensure participant understanding of the study and its procedures, participants will have as much time as they would like to consider their participation. Should they have questions, the consent form will provide contact information for the PI. Participation will be dependent upon consent; participants will not be able to continue to the survey unless they have consented to participate. 
 
To minimize the possibility of coercion or undue influence, the consent form will make it clear that participation is voluntary and that potential participants may choose not to participate without penalty; similarly, the consent form will make it clear that participants may withdraw their participation without penalty too. In addition, researchers will not use unduly influential or coercive language in recruitment materials. 
 
 
**Compensation:**   
 
Some participants will have the opportunity to enter a drawing for $50. Participants who opt in and provide a valid email address in the contact information survey will be eligible. The drawing will take place after data collection is complete, likely on or near Wednesday, December 9, 2020. We will choose at least one winner. Compensation will be issued via Venmo or PayPal.  
 
Other participants will have the opportunity to earn 0.5 credits in partial fulfillment of course requirements via the Psychology Department’s SONA credit participant pool. 
 
The level of compensation is expected to be adequate to incentivize participation without being unduly influential. Participants who submit a survey but indicate they wish to exclude their data from analyses will still be eligible for compensation. 
 
There are no costs to participants. 
 
**Potential Benefits to Participants:**  
 
There are no direct benefits to participants beyond the educational experience of participating and the knowledge that they are contributing to our understanding of human psychology. 
 
**Risks to Participants:** 
 
The risks to participants are minimal. Procedures are largely limited to responding to survey questions about meat consumption and providing demographic information. These are common everyday experiences. For participants taking part in exchange for entering a drawing as compensation, there is also a slight risk of a breach of confidentiality because we are collecting identifiers (names, email addresses) from the participants who wish to enter the compensation drawing. However, the data we are collecting would not be considered sensitive by reasonable standards, thus the severity of a breach, in the unlikely event one were to occur, would be quite low in magnitude. See Data Management and Confidentiality, section, for the steps we will take to mitigate this risk.  
 
**Withdrawal of Participants:** 
 
We will not withdraw participants from the research without their consent.  
 
If participants withdraw by indicating they would like us to exclude their data from the final data set, we will delete their responses when the data are downloaded from Qualtrics, prior to analysis or sharing in a public web repository. We will not be able to delete responses from any participants who may contact the PI after-the-fact because survey data files will not enable us to identify their specific responses. 
 
**Data Management and Confidentiality:** 
 
All information will be collected via Qualtrics surveys that are housed in the PI’s password-protected account. The data collection survey will only house participant data without personal identifiers; the contact information survey will only house participant identifiers (name, email address) without data.  
 
To mitigate the risk of a breach of confidentiality, we will not maintain a link between identifiers and data. In addition, only individuals who have been approved as study personnel under this protocol will be given collaborative access to the surveys through their Tufts password-protected Qualtrics account on an as-needed basis. 
 
Once data collection is complete, the PI will download the data and contact information from the two surveys and store them on a password-protected Tufts computer. After verifying that the data are deidentified, she will make the data available in a public web repository for access by other researchers, including the student researchers in her PSY 32 course. The data will, thus, be stored indefinitely.  
 
As soon as the PI has completed the compensation drawing process, she will delete the contact information from the computer and from Qualtrics to further mitigate risk of a breach of confidentiality. 
 
**Provisions to Protect the Privacy and Confidentiality of Participants and the Research Data:** 
 
Participants will complete this study on a computer with internet access at a time and location of their choosing. We are not asking them to provide sensitive, personal information. Survey items are innocuous questions about meat consumption and demographics, but participants are free to decline to answer as they wish. In addition, our data management plan, as articulated above, is designed to minimize the risk of a breach of confidentiality. As such, participant privacy is well-protected.  
  
 
**Data Sharing:** 
 
The deidentified data will be shared in a public web repository (e.g., Open Science Framework, github, or other) for access by anyone with an internet connection indefinitely. Other researchers may use the data to contribute to a meta-analysis of direct replications of the original study by Sparkman and Walton (2017), and some may download the data to see if they can reproduce our results or generate novel insights in new analyses.
